text: A few weeks after Lesson 30's encryption work, Microsoft Defender for Cloud flags caldwelldocsstorage with a high-severity recommendation: storage account public access should be disallowed. The account-level AllowBlobPublicAccess setting is enabled, and one container, invoices-shared, has its public access level set to Blob — meaning anyone with the right URL can read every invoice PDF in it with no authentication at all. This is exactly the live risk Chapter 5 described CSPM tooling as being built to catch.

Just flipping the setting off doesn't explain how it got turned on, so Caldwell's team pulls the Activity Log for the storage account and filters for Set Storage Account Properties operations. The change traces to a contractor's account three weeks earlier, around the same time an external auditor needed a batch of invoices for a compliance review. The contractor enabled public access for a quick, no-login link, meaning to turn it back off once the audit wrapped — and just like the hardcoded secret in Lesson 13, later never came.

Before remediating, the team confirms what was actually exposed. Querying the storage account's containers confirms invoices-shared is the only one with public access set, at the Blob level. Checking diagnostic logs for anonymous GET requests shows only hits from the auditor's known IP range in those three weeks — the exposure was real, but nothing suggests anyone else actually found it.

The fix happens at two levels. The account-level AllowBlobPublicAccess setting is the real kill switch — once it's off, no container on that account can be public no matter its own setting. The team also sets the container's own permission to off directly, so it reads clean to anyone who checks it later. For the next external share, the documented answer is a time-limited SAS token scoped to one blob, never a public container.

Remediating isn't the last step. The team forces a fresh assessment from the recommendation's details page in Defender for Cloud and confirms the resource now shows Healthy, rather than waiting on the next automatic refresh. To stop this from happening again regardless of who makes the next change, they add an Azure Policy with a deny effect on any storage account created or updated with public blob access enabled.

A real finding, a real root cause, a real fix confirmed by re-scanning instead of assumed. Lesson 32 closes out the course by tying this chapter's four lessons, and all seven chapters behind them, into one review.
